items.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: and then I threw her in with like real guys: Kenny Barron, Ron Carter, Lewis Nash, Fathead, Hank Crawford. I said look, if I’m going to make a record with her I want to make it with my guys, you know.

ctx.x: Okay. So that they go for your luck, but how would you get hooked up with like say Jane Monheit for instance? You didn’t like find her, right?

I’ll tell you. See like one thing, I’m 64. I’m not running for class president, I don’t care what anybody thinks basically, so if you ask me a question I’ll tell you the truth. Jane Monheit had been turned down by every major adult producer and record company that exists. By the time they called me, they sent me a demo tape, I turned her down too, the demo tape was terrible. But her manager, Maryann Topra said, “please come hear her in person.” Because I’m telling you, if I would have turned her down, the next…
Let me go backwards a little bit. Your employment with Atlantic came to an end?

items.title: Kenny Barron — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I asked Joel Dorn where the tapes are, and he had no idea.

ctx.x: It’s called Wolf. Who owned that one?

Who owned it? I don’t know. At the time, Joel Dorn was with it. I don’t know. This was – it was called TK Productions. The company went under right after we did that. So this record never came out. I asked Joel Dorn where the tapes are, and he had no idea. We did it at Atlantic Studios, because he was involved with Atlantic at the time. Those tapes are out there somewhere. I have no idea who has them.
1980, Golden Lotus. John Stubblefield, and you brought in my colleague at Rutgers, Steve Nelson, to play.
